summary: Sina Shahandeh addresses the gap between typical AutoResearch agents—which excel at coding puzzles, toy optimization, and supervised ML tasks—and the demands of real scientific discovery. While coding agents handle implementation and optimization well, they saturate because they lack 'research taste'—the ability to generate novel hypotheses. The scientific method (observe, question, hypothesize, experiment, learn) requires hypothesis generation as its core bottleneck, not memory or learning from mistakes. Radicait's demonstration problem is in-silico PET: generating PET scan images from CT scans using ML image translation with an encoder-decoder GAN. The clinical context is identifying cancerous lung nodules without performing expensive PET scans. The initial model used 2.5D convolutions (2D slices stacked as channels). Standard optimization saturates here—the agent won't propose radical architecture changes like 3D convolutions without intervention. The solution is explicit problem decomposition into a hierarchy of components: data, architecture, training loss, metrics, evidence, and peripheral scripts. This hierarchy is documented as linked markdown files visualized in Obsidian at multiple levels. Before the optimization loop, the agent generates improvement ideas across all components, producing potentially 100 different solutions. This scaffolds reasoning LLMs to make decisions about each component, enabling radical changes. The process can run adversarially or collaboratively with multiple agents reviewing plans. The agent loop incorporates multiple metric types including qualitative ones, and multimodal models (e.g., Gemini) can be invoked to review generated images for quality control. Peter Spinberger's Oracle CLI packages code and data for GPT-4.5 Pro to close the loop on hypothesis generation and critique. The critique pattern—'this is what we implemented, this is the outcome, does this make sense, what would you do next'—drives continuous improvement. A second example involves image registration—aligning CT and PET scans taken at different times, complicated by respiration, patient movement, and scanner differences. A key limitation is that current LLMs lack understanding of scientific images (e.g., identifying tiny changes like nodules), as they are not trained on scientific data. Shahandeh compares the hierarchical decomposition trick to chain-of-thought reasoning—both scale test-time compute to improve model performance. Future models with better post-training may need fewer such tricks.

sections.title: Introduction and the AutoResearch Challenge
sections.summary: Shahandeh introduces the gap between typical AutoResearch agents (referencing Karpathy's repo) and real scientific tasks. Coding agents excel at implementation but saturate because they run out of ideas or 'research taste,' while good humans keep improving. The core bottleneck is hypothesis generation.

sections.title: Scientific Method and the Hypothesis Bottleneck
sections.summary: The scientific method (observe, question, hypothesize, experiment, learn) requires hypothesis generation as its core bottleneck. Memory and learning from mistakes are largely solved by organizing patterns; what remains difficult is coming up with good hypotheses for coding agents to keep improving.

sections.title: In-Silico PET: CT-to-PET Translation Problem
sections.summary: Radicait's demonstration problem: generating PET scan images from CT scans using ML image translation (encoder-decoder GAN). Clinical context is identifying cancerous lung nodules. Initial model used 2.5D convolutions. Standard optimization saturates and won't propose radical changes like 3D convolutions without human intervention.

sections.title: Problem Decomposition and Hierarchy Generation
sections.summary: The solution is explicit problem decomposition into a hierarchy of components (data, architecture, training loss, metrics, evidence, peripheral scripts). This hierarchy is documented as linked markdown files visualized in Obsidian at multiple levels, scaffolding the agent's step-by-step reasoning across all components.

sections.title: Hypothesis Generation and the Agent Loop
sections.summary: With the hierarchy in place, the agent generates approximately 100 candidate solutions modifying every component, enabling radical changes like 3D convolutions. Plans can be reviewed adversarially or collaboratively. The overall loop: codebase, metrics, goal achieved? no, hypothesize change, implement, repeat.

sections.title: Image Registration Example
sections.summary: A second example: image registration aligning CT and PET scans taken at different times. Challenges include respiration, patient movement, and different scanner positioning. This similarly requires navigating many metrics and potential failure modes in a long optimization process.

sections.title: Multimodal Review, Critique Loops, and Future Outlook
sections.summary: The agent loop uses multiple metric types (qualitative and quantitative) and can invoke multimodal models like Gemini for image quality control. Peter Spinberger's Oracle CLI packages code and data for GPT-4.5 Pro to close the loop on hypothesis generation and critique ('this is what we implemented, this is the outcome, does this make sense, what would you do next?'). Current LLMs lack understanding of scientific images (e.g., identifying nodules) because they aren't trained on scientific data—the biggest bottleneck for full autonomy. The hierarchical decomposition trick is compared to chain-of-thought reasoning as a way to scale test-time compute. Future models with better post-training may need fewer such tricks.
